questions.prompt: Why does NetFlow often prove more useful than full packet capture in practice?
options: It captures more detail per connection
Flow records are small enough to retain for months, so they still exist when an investigation begins weeks later -- PCAP at scale fills storage in days
It requires no sensors to collect
questions.explanation: The value of an evidence source is not only its detail but how long it survives. A perfect record that expired before you looked is worth less than a partial one still available.

questions.prompt: Why is workstation-to-workstation traffic on port 445 notable?
options: Endpoints normally talk to servers rather than to each other, so peer-to-peer SMB is abnormal in most environments and indicates lateral movement
It always indicates a misconfigured firewall
questions.explanation: East-west connectivity between endpoints breaks the normal hub-and-spoke pattern, and flow data shows it across the whole environment in a way host-by-host telemetry does not.

questions.prompt: What is the blind spot in an environment that collects flow only at the perimeter?
options: It cannot see any outbound traffic
Lateral movement is east-west and never crosses the boundary, so the initial callout and eventual exfiltration are visible while everything between them is not
Perimeter flow records lack byte counts
questions.explanation: Internal flow collection at core switches, or cloud VPC/NSG flow logs, is what makes the middle of an intrusion visible.

questions.prompt: What can flow data establish about exfiltration, and what can it not?
options: Both the content and the volume of what left
The volume, destination, and timing -- a defensible upper bound -- but not the content, since there is no payload
Only the destination, never the volume
questions.explanation: This maps directly onto the three-tier scope statement: flow supports 'a transfer of this size went here at this time' rather than a content inventory, and reporting it as more is where scope statements go wrong.
